\section[o rapto]{o rapto — the kidnapping, the abduction}

\label{lesson:PT-C291-rapto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the threat, then the Portuguese for the murderer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o rapto}
\textbf{o rapto} — \textquotedblleft{}the kidnapping, the abduction\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O rapto do empresário foi notícia em toda a cidade.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The businessman’s kidnapping was news all over the city.}
\end{quote}

\emph{O rapto de uma criança} — a child abduction.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rapto} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{raptus} \textquotedblleft{}a carrying off\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{rapere} \textquotedblleft{}to seize, to snatch\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o rapto}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o rapto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o rapto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the threat, then the Portuguese for the murderer, then say \emph{o rapto} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o rapto mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The kidnapping, the abduction\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[raptar]{raptar — to kidnap, to abduct}

\label{lesson:PT-C291-raptar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the murderer, then the Portuguese for the kidnapping.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: raptar}
\textbf{raptar} — \textquotedblleft{}to kidnap, to abduct\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Os homens raptaram o filho do empresário.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The men kidnapped the businessman’s son.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Raptar alguém} — to kidnap someone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{raptar} is built on \emph{rapto} \textquotedblleft{}a kidnapping\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{raptus}, from \emph{rapere} \textquotedblleft{}to seize\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o sequestro]{o sequestro — the hostage-taking, the kidnapping; the hijacking}

\label{lesson:PT-C291-sequestro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the kidnapping, then the Portuguese for to kidnap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o sequestro}
\textbf{o sequestro} — \textquotedblleft{}the hostage-taking, the kidnapping; the hijacking\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O sequestro do avião durou dez horas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The hijacking of the plane lasted ten hours.}
\end{quote}

In Brazil the usual word for a kidnapping.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sequestro} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{sequestrum} \textquotedblleft{}a deposit placed in trust\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{sequester} \textquotedblleft{}a go-between, a trustee\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o sequestro}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o sequestro}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o sequestro}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the kidnapping, then the Portuguese for to kidnap, then say \emph{o sequestro} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o sequestro mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The hostage-taking, the kidnapping; the hijacking\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[sequestrar]{sequestrar — to hold hostage, to kidnap; to hijack}

\label{lesson:PT-C291-sequestrar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to kidnap, then the Portuguese for the hostage-taking.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sequestrar}
\textbf{sequestrar} — \textquotedblleft{}to hold hostage, to kidnap; to hijack\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Sequestraram um autocarro com vinte pessoas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They hijacked a bus with twenty people on it.}
\end{quote}

In court language: \emph{sequestrar bens} — to seize goods.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sequestrar} is a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{sequestrāre} \textquotedblleft{}to put aside, to hold in trust\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{sequester} \textquotedblleft{}a trustee\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to kidnap, then the Portuguese for the hostage-taking, then say \emph{sequestrar} again

\section[o refém]{o refém — the hostage}

\label{lesson:PT-C291-refem}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the hostage-taking, then the Portuguese for to hold hostage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o refém}
\textbf{o refém} — \textquotedblleft{}the hostage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O refém voltou para casa ao fim de dois dias.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The hostage went back home after two days.}
\end{quote}

The same form for a woman: \emph{a refém}. Plural \emph{reféns}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{refém} comes from Arabic \emph{rahīn} \textquotedblleft{}a pledge, a hostage\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
